title: Underhanded trickery
core: All four cover getting an advantage by deceiving someone rather than overpowering them — the win comes from misdirection, concealment or clever manoeuvring. They split on three axes: **scale** (a whole practice of cheating vs. one move), **legitimacy** (flatly dishonest vs. fair play), and **register** (indictment vs. newspaper column). Two of them name a kind of dishonesty; two name a single tactic, only one of which is even wrong.

words.nuance: The only one where the **rules themselves are the weapon** — loopholes, quibbles, fine print, procedural sleight-of-hand. **Chicanery** stays technically legal, which is the whole point of the contempt; it's the professional's word (lawyers, accountants, election officials) for someone who won disgracefully but can't be charged.

Not technically legal at all — **skullduggery** is plainly shady, done out of sight: backroom deals, quiet double-crosses, a rigged committee. What marks it is tone, not method: it's informal and half-amused where *fraud* is prosecutorial, and it's the word for wrongdoing you suspect but cannot prove.

A unit, not a practice — **one small move** with a hidden motive, not a pattern of dishonesty. It's the cheapest and most trivial of the group (a marketing ploy, a ploy to keep you on the call), and calling something a ploy already announces you've seen through it.

The only honest one. A **feint** is deception the opponent is *meant to notice* — it fails if nobody takes the bait — so boxers, fencers and generals do it inside the rules and nobody calls it cheating. It's also the most physical: a committed-looking movement in the wrong direction so the real strike lands.

exam_note: The trap is treating all four as pejorative — sentences about sport, negotiation or war want the sanctioned *feint*, while a sentence whose deception is legal-but-slimy wants *chicanery*, not *skullduggery*.
